es.text: Matar dos pájaros de un tiro
es.literal: to kill two birds with one shot
es.meaning: To achieve two aims with a single action.
es.example: Voy al supermercado de camino al trabajo, así mato dos pájaros de un tiro.
es.exampleTranslation: I stop at the store on the way to work — two birds, one stone.

it.text: Prendere due piccioni con una fava
it.literal: to catch two pigeons with one bean
it.meaning: To achieve two aims with a single action.
it.example: Se vado al lavoro in bicicletta, faccio esercizio fisico e risparmio sulla benzina: così prendo due piccioni con una fava!
it.exampleTranslation: If I bike to work, I get exercise and save on gas — two birds with one stone!

bridge.note: Spanish mirrors English almost exactly. Italian baits one bean to catch two birds — the older form of the metaphor, traceable to the 1612 Crusca. prendere (catch) is gentler than matar (kill).

interference.es_to_it: 'Uccidere due uccelli con un colpo' is a literal translation, not the idiom. Italian catches two pigeons with one bean: prendere due piccioni con una fava.
interference.it_to_es: Two problems at once. Coger is vulgar across Mexico and the Río de la Plata, where the sexual sense dominates — speakers there reach for agarrar or tomar. And the Spanish idiom kills birds with a shot anyway: matar dos pájaros de un tiro.
